question: India's installed non-fossil capacity is growing fast, yet the grid is struggling to absorb it. Examine the challenges of integrating renewable energy and suggest measures to make the transition reliable and just.
why: Energy has been asked in every sitting since 2008 (24 questions). Past questions asked what the sources are and what policy exists; 'grid integration, storage and just transition' has not been asked yet and is where the commission is moving.
intro: India has set a target of 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030 and net zero by 2070. Solar and wind are variable, so a fast-growing share of them stresses a grid that was designed around steady coal power.

pts: Variability and intermittency: solar peaks at noon, demand peaks in the evening ('duck curve').
Transmission gaps: best sites (Rajasthan, Gujarat, Anantapur–Kurnool belt) are far from load centres; curtailment risk.
Weak distribution companies: payment delays and poor finances discourage power purchase.
Storage shortage and import dependence for solar cells, modules and battery minerals.
Land, water and community issues around large solar parks.
Storage: pumped hydro and battery storage with viability support; solar-plus-storage tenders.
Green Energy Corridors and inter-state transmission waivers for renewables.
Market tools: real-time and ancillary markets, time-of-day tariffs, demand response.
Domestic manufacturing through the PLI scheme for solar modules and batteries.
Distributed generation: PM Surya Ghar rooftop solar and PM-KUSUM for farm feeders.
Just transition: re-skilling coal-region workers and a District Mineral Foundation role.
Large solar and wind capacity, pumped-storage and green-hydrogen proposals; coastline and port access are an advantage.

conclusion: A reliable transition needs storage, wires and finances to grow along with capacity. A grid that is flexible and a transition that is fair to coal workers will decide whether the targets deliver secure power.
updates: Latest non-fossil capacity figure and share in the mix (MNRE / CEA dashboard)
Status of the battery-storage and pumped-storage tenders and the viability gap funding scheme
PM Surya Ghar and PM-KUSUM progress; Andhra Pradesh's latest renewable and green-hydrogen policy

question: Space is now opening to private players in India. Discuss the opportunities and challenges before the Indian space sector after the creation of IN-SPACe.
why: Space and satellites are among the top recurring themes (23 questions, asked in every sitting). Questions so far were on uses of satellites and ISRO achievements; the 'private participation and challenges' dimension is new.
intro: The 2020 reforms opened space activities to non-government entities, with IN-SPACe as the single-window regulator and NSIL as the commercial arm of ISRO. India now hopes to grow its share of the global space economy from a very small base.

pts: Cost advantage and a record of low-cost missions (Chandrayaan, Mangalyaan).
Start-ups in launch vehicles and satellites (for example Skyroot and Agnikul) and Sriharikota's launch infrastructure.
Applications: communication, remote sensing, navigation (NavIC), agriculture, disaster warning.
Defence and strategic uses; export of small-satellite launches by PSLV and SSLV.
Small private capital and long gestation; limited insurance and liability law.
Absence of a comprehensive space law; clarity on spectrum, licensing and liability is still evolving.
Dependence on foreign components and shortage of launch slots.
Space debris and sustainability concerns.
Pass a clear space activities law; support start-ups through the venture fund and test facilities.
Public–private model for launch, with ISRO focused on research and human spaceflight (Gaganyaan).

conclusion: The sector can move from being state-led to being state-enabled. A predictable legal framework and steady funding will convert India's low-cost advantage into a larger commercial share.
updates: Recent ISRO launches and the Gaganyaan schedule
Space-sector FDI limits and the Space Activities Bill status
Chandrayaan / Aditya-L1 / NISAR follow-ups and any 2026 missions

question: Antimicrobial resistance is called a silent pandemic. Explain how it arises and discuss the policy measures needed to contain it in India.
why: Infectious diseases have been asked 23 times, nearly always as 'describe the disease and its prevention'. The policy angle (AMR, One Health, surveillance) has never been asked and is current in health policy debates.
intro: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) occurs when bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites stop responding to medicines. India is among the largest consumers of antibiotics, and misuse across humans, animals and agriculture speeds up resistance.

pts: Over-the-counter and incomplete antibiotic courses; self-medication.
Antibiotic use in poultry, dairy and aquaculture as growth promoters; residues in the environment and in effluent from drug factories.
Poor hospital infection control and sanitation spread resistant strains.
Natural selection and gene transfer between bacteria.
National Action Plan on AMR (2017) and the One Health approach.
Schedule H1 and ban on certain fixed-dose combinations; restrictions on colistin in animals.
Surveillance networks (ICMR AMRSN) and antibiotic stewardship in hospitals.
Vaccination, WASH, and rapid diagnostics to cut antibiotic need.
R&D incentives for new antibiotics and phage therapy; global cooperation (WHO Global Action Plan).

conclusion: AMR can undo decades of progress in treating infections. Prudent use, strong surveillance and a One Health approach are cheaper than the future cost of untreatable infections.
updates: Status of India's National Action Plan on AMR 2.0
Latest ICMR AMR surveillance report
Any new antibiotic approvals or national diagnostic schemes

question: Biodiversity loss is a development challenge as much as an ecological one. Discuss the measures taken by India to conserve biodiversity and suggest a way forward.
why: Biodiversity has 22 questions, mostly 'importance, threats, hotspots'. Policy and community-led measures (Biological Diversity Act, 30x30, BMCs) are not yet asked.
intro: India holds around 8 per cent of the world's recorded species on about 2.4 per cent of its land and includes four global biodiversity hotspots (Himalaya, Indo-Burma, Western Ghats and Sundaland-Nicobar). Habitat loss, invasive species, pollution and climate change are shrinking this base.

pts: In-situ: national parks, sanctuaries, biosphere reserves, tiger and elephant projects, community reserves.
Ex-situ: botanical and zoological gardens, gene banks (NBPGR), seed banks.
Law: Wildlife Protection Act 1972, Forest Conservation Act, Biological Diversity Act 2002 with Biodiversity Management Committees and access-and-benefit-sharing.
International: CBD, CITES, Ramsar, Nagoya Protocol and the Kunming-Montreal Framework (30 by 30).
Community and tech-based: people's biodiversity registers, Joint Forest Management, camera traps and satellite monitoring.
Corridors to connect fragmented habitats; restoration of degraded land.
Integrate biodiversity in project clearance and offsets; strengthen BMC funding.
Green finance and payments for ecosystem services; protect traditional knowledge.
Andhra Pradesh: Eastern Ghats, Kolleru, Coringa mangroves and Pulicat need focused management.

conclusion: Conservation works when people living near the resource benefit from it. Law, science and community stewardship together can reconcile growth with a living natural base.
updates: Latest tiger/elephant census data and new Ramsar sites
Biological Diversity (Amendment) Act 2023 changes and rules
India's updated National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan

question: Evaluate the Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016 and the Swachh Bharat Mission (Urban) 2.0 in the light of the waste hierarchy. What more is needed to make Indian cities 'garbage free'?
why: Waste management is a recurring theme (types, impacts, recycling). The policy-evaluation framing (SWM Rules 2016, EPR, SBM-U 2.0) is a likely new dimension.
intro: Indian cities generate a very large quantity of municipal solid waste every day, and legacy dumpsites such as Deonar and Ghazipur have become a symbol of failure. The rules and missions try to move the system from dumping to a circular economy.

pts: SWM Rules 2016: segregation at source into wet, dry and hazardous; user charges; extended producer responsibility; waste-to-energy; bio-mining of legacy waste.
SBM-U 2.0 (2021–26): garbage-free cities, remediation of legacy dumpsites, source segregation, processing 100 per cent of waste.
Plastic Waste, E-waste and Battery rules with EPR certificates.
Gains: more households covered by door-to-door collection; rise in processing; swachh rankings improved awareness.
Gaps: low segregation, weak urban local body finances, informal waste-pickers excluded, limited landfill capacity, mixed-waste incineration quality problems.
Decentralised composting and biogas (Indore model), incentives for segregation.
Integrate waste-pickers; enforce EPR; promote reuse and repair; scientific landfill with leachate treatment.

conclusion: A garbage-free city is built on segregation at the doorstep and accountability along the chain. Following the waste hierarchy of reduce, reuse and recycle will cost less than managing dumpsites.
updates: SBM-U 2.0 progress dashboard and legacy-waste remediation numbers
Recent amendments to Plastic Waste / E-waste / Battery rules and EPR targets
Andhra Pradesh Swachh Andhra initiatives and city ranking

question: With the rise of AI-generated deepfakes and online financial fraud, discuss the cyber-security framework in India. How adequate is it, and what changes are needed?
why: ICT questions are asked every sitting (24), and cyber crime has appeared in 2020, 2023 and 2025. Questions have been about types of cyber crime; the 'framework adequacy and AI-enabled threats' angle is next.
intro: India has one of the largest digital populations and real-time payments systems, which makes it a prime target for ransomware, phishing and AI-enabled fraud such as deepfakes and voice cloning.

pts: Information Technology Act 2000 (sections on hacking, identity theft, publishing obscene content) and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023.
CERT-In for incident response; National Cyber Security Policy 2013; National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre (NCIIPC).
I4C and the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal (helpline 1930); the Sanchar Saathi platform.
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita provisions for fraud and impersonation.
Law is older than current threats; no specific provision for deepfakes or AI harms.
Low reporting, slow forensic labs and a shortage of trained police.
Cross-border crime needs data access treaties; platform accountability is limited.
Update the IT Act; AI-labelling and watermarking rules; platform liability.
Capacity building: cyber forensics, state cyber cells; public awareness and digital literacy.
International cooperation (Budapest Convention debate, UN cybercrime treaty) and critical-infrastructure audits.

conclusion: Technology that expands inclusion must be matched by trust. A modern law, capable enforcement and an aware citizen will keep India's digital public goods safe.
updates: Status of the Digital India Act and the DPDP Rules
Latest CERT-In / I4C numbers on cyber fraud
Government rules or advisories on deepfakes and AI labelling

question: Discuss India's climate commitments under the Paris Agreement and its updated NDC. Is the principle of 'common but differentiated responsibilities' under pressure?
why: Climate has appeared 16 times (COP summits, global warming effects). Questions on CBDR-RC, climate finance and India's NDC delivery have not been asked.
intro: India contributes a small share of historical emissions and has low per-capita emissions, but is among the largest emitters in absolute terms and highly vulnerable. At COP26 India announced a Panchamrit plan with net zero by 2070.

pts: Non-fossil capacity of 500 GW and 50 per cent of power from non-fossil by 2030.
Reduction in emissions intensity of GDP (45 per cent from 2005 levels by 2030) and a carbon sink of 2.5–3 billion tonnes through forests.
Mission LiFE for sustainable lifestyles; National Green Hydrogen Mission; Indian carbon market under the Energy Conservation Amendment Act.
Developed countries have missed the 100 billion dollar finance promise; the new collective goal for finance is contested.
Carbon border adjustment (EU CBAM) taxes developing-country exports.
Pressure to phase out coal while finance and technology are not forthcoming.
Insist on climate finance, adaptation funding and loss and damage; build domestic markets and green industry; strengthen adaptation in agriculture and cities.

conclusion: India's position that development must not be sacrificed to climate action is legitimate, but its own interest also lies in a cleaner path. Equity and ambition must advance together.
updates: Outcomes of the latest COP and India's submitted NDC
Status of the Indian Carbon Credit Trading Scheme
Latest climate finance goal (NCQG) and EU CBAM rollout

question: India is called the 'pharmacy of the world' and a major vaccine producer. Discuss the evolution of vaccine technology and the issues in India's universal immunisation programme.
why: Vaccines were asked 15 times, always as concept (immunity, how a vaccine is made). The delivery-system dimension (UIP, Mission Indradhanush, mRNA, cold chain) is unseen.
intro: Vaccination prevents an estimated millions of deaths each year. India runs one of the world's largest immunisation programmes and produces a large share of the world's vaccines for children.

pts: Live-attenuated and inactivated vaccines (BCG, polio, DPT).
Subunit, conjugate and toxoid vaccines (hepatitis B, pneumococcal).
Recombinant DNA and viral-vector vaccines; mRNA vaccines and nucleic-acid platforms (rapid design).
Nasal vaccines and needle-free delivery; indigenous Covaxin, ZyCoV-D and HPV vaccine Cervavac.
UIP covers vaccines for 12 diseases; Mission Indradhanush and U-WIN digital registry to reach left-out children.
Issues: dropouts and zero-dose children, cold-chain gaps, hesitancy and misinformation, urban slums, regulatory approvals.
Digital tracking, community mobilisation by ASHA workers, local manufacturing of novel platforms, strengthening pharmacovigilance.

conclusion: Vaccines are among the most cost-effective public health tools. Reaching the last child with a safe, cold-chained dose matters as much as inventing the next vaccine.
updates: Newly added vaccines in UIP (HPV, others) and coverage data from NFHS
Any new indigenous vaccine approvals
Current status of mRNA vaccine research in India

question: Discuss the issues of patenting in agriculture and pharmaceuticals in India. How does the Indian patent regime balance innovation and public interest?
why: IPR is a small but constant theme (6 questions). Evergreening, compulsory licensing and seed patents are classic issue-angles not yet asked in the AP series.
intro: Following TRIPS, India amended its Patents Act (2005 amendment restored product patents). The law tries to reward innovators while keeping medicines affordable and farmers' rights intact.

pts: Section 3(d): no patent for new forms of known substances without enhanced efficacy (Novartis v. Union of India 2013).
Compulsory licensing (Natco-Bayer 2012) and Section 92 for public health emergencies; Doha Declaration flexibilities.
Plants and animals are excluded from patentability; PPV&FR Act 2001 protects farmers' rights and breeders' rights.
Evergreening, pay-for-delay and trade-pressure to dilute safeguards in FTAs.
Biopiracy (neem, turmeric, basmati) and the role of the Traditional Knowledge Digital Library.
Seed industry control, GM crops and patent claims on traits; small farmers' access.
Use TRIPS flexibilities; strengthen patent examination; protect traditional knowledge; incentivise public-funded research.

conclusion: A patent system is a bargain between inventor and society. India's safeguards show that protection and access can co-exist if they are enforced with care.
updates: India's IPR policy updates and any FTA IPR chapters (UK, EU, EFTA)
Recent compulsory licensing or patent opposition cases
GI tag registrations from Andhra Pradesh

question: Coastal Andhra Pradesh faces repeated cyclones and floods. Describe the institutional framework for disaster management in India and suggest a resilience strategy for the state's coast.
why: Disaster management has 13 questions. The institutional (NDMA, SDMA, Sendai) framework and a state-specific resilience strategy for AP's 974 km coast fit the AP-focus of recent papers.
intro: Andhra Pradesh has one of the longest coastlines in India and is exposed to cyclones, storm surges and river floods. The Disaster Management Act 2005 moved India from relief-centric to a preparedness and mitigation approach.

pts: NDMA, State Disaster Management Authorities and District Disaster Management Authorities; NDRF and SDRF; NIDM for training.
National Disaster Management Plan 2019 aligned with the Sendai Framework (2015–2030).
Funding: NDRF/SDRF and mitigation funds; Finance Commission recommendations.
Early warning by IMD and Aadhaar-linked alerts; cyclone shelters and evacuation roads.
Coastal Regulation Zone enforcement, mangrove and shelterbelt restoration (Coringa), saline embankments.
Resilient housing, power and telecom lines; flood forecasting for Godavari and Krishna with reservoir operation.
Community training and the role of local bodies; insurance and livelihoods recovery.

conclusion: Each cyclone saved lives because warning and evacuation have improved. The next step is to protect livelihoods and infrastructure through resilient design and mangrove buffers.
updates: Recent cyclone/flood events affecting AP and the response
Latest NDMA guidelines and the Disaster Management (Amendment) Act 2025
AP State Disaster Management Plan updates and the National Cyclone Risk Mitigation Project
